newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: Tajik govt, Islamists take stride towards peace.
newsitem.headline: Tajik govt, Islamists take stride towards peace.

text.p: The former Soviet republic of Tajikistan took a big step towards lasting peace after four years of civil war when the government agreed on Sunday to legalise major Islamist opposition parties and media.

The deal, part of a planned comprehensive peace settlement, was signed by Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov and opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri after two days of difficult talks in Bishkek, capital of neighbouring Kyrgyzstan.
They also agreed on an amnesty and exchange of prisoners.
"At last the Tajiks have come to their senses and realised how deadly is further confrontation for their nation and Islam," Nuri said after the signing.
"Thanks to the Bishkek meeting, inter-Tajik negotiations enter their final stage which makes it possible to bring peace to the suffering Tajik land," Rakhmonov said.
Rakhmonov and Nuri -- arch-foes in the recent past -- gave each other a brotherly hug a few moments later.

Last December, Rakhmonov's secular government and the Islamists agreed a ceasefire to end four years of civil war which killed tens of thousands of people in the Central Asian state and drove many more from their homes.
Military terms for the peace deal and a power-sharing agreement have been agreed.
But legalisation of the opposition and its press, as well as the amnesty, were the main obstacles blocking the talks mediated by the United Nations, Russia and Iran.

The political protocol signed in Bishkek provides for legalisation of Tajikistan's three main parties -- including the leading opposition force, the Islamist Party of Revival-- and of the opposition press.

The opposition would have to disband most of its armed units first. But a memorandum summing up the results of the talks said the opposition would be allowed to station up to 500 of its fighters in the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
The two sides have yet to agree on how many opposition representatives will be brought into the government.

Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev, who praised Rakhmonov and Nuri for "rising above personal ambitions", said that a special envoy of U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan would fly to Iran to arrange a meeting of both delegations as soon as possible.
The meeting must work out concrete ways to implement the political protocol.
Akayev said a "General Agreement on Peace and National Accord in Tajikistan" could be signed in Moscow no later than the first half of June.
